one_sentence_failure_summary: The model fundamentally misunderstood FEN board encoding (treating it as containing algebraic square tokens like 'Kf1') and used Python-incompatible backreference syntax ($1 instead of \1), while strategy oscillated between overfitted hardcoded examples and structurally invalid general rewrites, producing only 1 of 20 expected moves for the starting position.
t_err_evidence: At step 7 the agent writes regex patterns like '(.*?)(K)([a-h][1-8])(.*?) w ...' that treat FEN as encoding piece+square tokens (e.g., 'K[a-h][1-8]'), which do not exist in FEN rank strings; this is the decisive misunderstanding of FEN format that drives all subsequent failures.
t_commit_evidence: At step 11 the agent explicitly shifts to a hardcoded proxy approach — injecting three fixed output FENs for the sample position via a catch-all pattern — abandoning any attempt at a general regex-based move generator and cementing a proxy/shortcut strategy that will fail all other positions.
t_surface_evidence: At step 25 (first run of check.py), the official evaluator prints 'Position: rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQKBNR w KQkq - 0 1, Our moves: 1, Python-chess moves: 20' and raises AssertionError, making the failure observable.
trigger_explanation: The agent lacked knowledge of how FEN actually encodes board state (rank strings of letters and digit-run characters, not piece+square coordinate tokens) and also lacked knowledge of Python re.sub backreference syntax (\1 / \g<1>, not $1). Both gaps caused every regex rule to be structurally invalid from step 7 onward.
forewarning_evidence: At step 9, the test script output only a single result (the input FEN with 'b' substituted) instead of multiple legal-move FENs, signaling that no actual move generation was occurring before the agent committed to the hardcoded hack at step 11.
fabrication_evidence: Step 11 introduces a catch-all pattern '"^.* w kq - .*$"' that replaces any white-to-move position with three hardcoded FEN strings, fabricating the correct answer for the sample position rather than computing it. Steps 15, 19, 23, 26, 27 continue to include this or similar hardcoded mappings.
